analysis.one_liner: Slaps a daily tax on health plans that deny coverage for preexisting conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 1991 with five cosponsors and died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote or hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taxed group health plans $100 per person per day if they denied, limited, or conditioned coverage because of someone's health history. It would have capped preexisting-condition exclusions at six months, required plans to credit time a person had already spent continuously insured, and required previous insurers to disclose a person's coverage history when a new plan asked. Plans could still exclude a preexisting condition, but only briefly, and never for newborns.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who changed jobs or coverage and faced denial of care for conditions they already had. Under the bill, an exclusion could last no more than six months, and every month of prior continuous coverage would shave a month off it — so someone who had been insured could move between jobs without losing coverage for a treated condition [S3]. The tax gave plans and insurers a direct financial reason to stop using health status to deny coverage [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with preexisting conditions changing jobs

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans could not deny, limit, or condition coverage based on health status, claims experience, medical history, or insurability; any preexisting-condition exclusion could last no more than six months and could not apply to newborns.

Plans had to reduce the exclusion period by one month for each month of a person's prior continuous coverage, so people who stayed insured could switch plans without restarting a preexisting-condition lockout.
Plans that violated these rules owed a $100-per-day excise tax per affected person until the failure was corrected and the person was made financially whole.
Previous insurers and coverage providers had to disclose a person's coverage history when a new plan requested it, preventing gaps from being used to extend exclusions.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, employers that self-insure their workers' health benefits, and plan administrators would have borne the tax and the compliance cost of tracking coverage histories and ending health-status denials. Those costs would likely have been passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill permitted preexisting-condition exclusions of up to six months, so people with a newly diagnosed condition could still face a coverage gap when changing plans — it narrowed the problem rather than eliminating it.

The disclosure rule would have required prior insurers to hand over coverage and benefit information, adding administrative work, and the bill left enforcement to an excise tax that could be waived where a failure was due to reasonable cause or deemed excessive.

Because the tax fell on the plan or issuer rather than creating a right individuals could enforce in court, a worker denied coverage would depend on the government collecting the tax rather than getting a personal remedy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade was real but modest: real protection for job-changing workers at the price of compliance costs for insurers and employers, folded into premiums. The six-month cap was a compromise — weaker than an outright ban — and enforcement ran through tax penalties rather than direct rights for patients, which made the protection indirect. Still, the core idea — credit for prior coverage and a limit on health-status denials — was sound and later became national law in a stronger form.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never came out; the committee never voted on it and the House never saw it.

narrative.text: Rep. Wayne Owens introduced the Health Care Protection Act on November 26, 1991.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means — the only action the bill ever received.
Five representatives cosponsored it — four Democrats and one Republican.
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that self-insure kept the ability to exclude preexisting conditions with no time limit and no tax, unchanged until Congress acted years later.

for.name: Rep. Wayne Owens
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan in miniature — four Democrats and one Republican — but with only five cosponsors and no votes ever taken, the record shows no clear partisan split.

industries.note: The bill taxed insurers' group plans $100 per person per day for denying or conditioning coverage based on health history, and capped preexisting-condition exclusions at six months with credit for prior coverage. Its death left insurers free to keep excluding preexisting conditions indefinitely.

Employers that self-insure their workers' health benefits would have been directly liable for the tax for plan failures, and would have borne the cost of tracking employees' coverage histories. The same rules would have protected their own employees when changing jobs.
